props.name: commercial 'zinc chromate' is a mixture of (A) and (B); Hanawalt's ZnCrO4 is (B)
props.note: Hanawalt's data are cited (ref. 8); the commercial sample's measurement is the authors'
props.statement: The X-ray pattern of a domestic commercial 'Zinc chromate' is a mixture of (A) and (B), not true ZnCrO4; the spacings Hanawalt gives for 'ZnCrO4' are exactly those of (B), not of ZnCrO4.

props.name: CrO3 calcination: intermediate lines, then Cr2O3 at 600 °C
props.statement: Products of CrO3 calcined at 250 °C or below are too hygroscopic to photograph; after the decomposition near 300 °C they are not hygroscopic. At 355 and 450 °C they contain lines of neither CrO3 nor Cr2O3, which weaken at higher temperature while the Cr2O3 lines grow, giving almost complete Cr2O3 at 600 °C.

props.name: CrO3 decomposes via Cr2O5 to Cr2O3
props.note: 'Cr205' and 'Cr盆03' are the text layer's renderings of Cr2O5 and Cr2O3
props.statement: The thermobalance results for CrO3 alone agree fairly well with those of Honda and Vasenin and show that CrO3 becomes Cr2O3 via Cr2O5.

props.name: assignment of the CrO3 thermal changes
props.statement: Chromic anhydride alone shows five marked changes E, F, G, H and I: E is the release of free water, G, H and I correspond to the decompositions C, D and E of Fig. 1, and F is the endothermic heat of fusion at the melting point of chromic anhydride, without weight change.

props.name: thermal changes are irreversible
props.statement: In every sample decomposition occurs as the temperature rises, but no change is seen on cooling, so the changes are irreversible; zinc oxide alone shows no thermal change.

props.name: B, C and D series of thermal changes for Zn/Cr > 1
props.statement: For Zn/Cr > 1, apart from A of 1.5:1, there are a B series of changes from about 270-280 °C, a C series at about 320-330 °C and a D series near 480 °C; the B series is largest at 4:1, the C series at 2:1, and the D series grows as Cr increases. The two different decompositions (B, C) were not clearly discernible in the thermobalance curves.

props.name: excess CrO3 is mixed in its original form
props.statement: At Zn:Cr = 1:5 the decompositions corresponding to G and I are clearly seen and at 1:2 no marked change; the trend differs clearly from Zn/Cr > 1, and it is almost certain that the excess chromic anhydride is mixed in its original form.

props.name: B and C are dehydrations, D a deoxygenation following 2CrO3 = Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2
props.statement: The products of the thermal changes are: A dehydration, B and C series dehydration, D series deoxygenation; the oxygen released equals the amount calculated for decomposition of the added chromic anhydride by 2CrO3 = Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2, and the water of the B and C series corresponds to 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O at 4:1 and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O at 2:1.

props.name: calcination at 700 °C gives ZnCr2O4 spinel
props.note: the comparison with coprecipitated catalysts refers to cited work (ref. 9)
props.statement: After calcination at 700 °C for 2 h, Zn:Cr = 1:2 shows the characteristic lines of ZnCr2O4 spinel, as with catalysts prepared from coprecipitates; with more zinc, ZnO lines appear besides the spinel, and with more chromium, Cr2O3 lines appear (Table 3). This proves that oxygen is released according to equation (1) and chromium goes from hexavalent to trivalent.

props.name: summary: 4:1 and 2:1 hydrates lose water and oxygen endothermically
props.statement: For Zn/Cr >= 1, the 4:1 and 2:1 materials have definite X-ray structures corresponding to 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O; the crystal water of the former is released endothermically at 270-280 °C and of the latter at 320-330 °C, and at 470-480 °C endothermic deoxygenation releases the oxygen corresponding to 2CrO3 -> Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2. Above Zn/Cr = 1 in Cr, excess CrO3 appears to be mixed as it is; after 700 °C, 2 h, Zn:Cr = 1:2 forms the spinel, with ZnO lines when Zn is richer and Cr2O3 lines when Cr is richer.

props.name: thermal decomposition in air differs for Zn/Cr > 1, = 1 and < 1
props.statement: On heating in air, catalysts with Zn/Cr > 1 decompose near 300 °C and near 500 °C with nearly the same trend; Zn/Cr = 1 shows decomposition at 150-200 °C and a very broad decomposition from about 400 to 550 °C; Zn/Cr < 1 shows a new decomposition near 370 °C; zinc oxide alone loses no weight up to 650 °C; CrO3 alone shows three decompositions between about 270 and 470 °C.

props.name: Zn:Cr = 1:1 divides the catalysts into two systems
props.statement: The catalysts divide at Zn:Cr = 1:1 into two systems: for Zn/Cr > 1 the decomposition curves appear in neither zinc oxide nor chromic anhydride, so they cannot be simple mixtures; for Zn/Cr <= 1 the curves approach that of chromic anhydride alone as more is added, so the chromic anhydride in excess of Zn:Cr = 1:1 is mixed in as it is.

props.name: only 4:1 and 2:1 have a definite X-ray structure
props.note: the ratios are printed '1.4:1' and '211' in the garbled text layer; read as 4:1 and 2:1
props.statement: In the uncalcined catalysts the zinc oxide lines weaken with increasing Cr while new lines (A) strengthen, and at Zn:Cr = 4:1 only (A) remains; with more Cr (A) weakens and (B) strengthens, strongest at 2:1; with still more Cr lines (C), thought to be a dichromate, appear. Of the Zn/Cr >= 1 catalysts only 4:1 and 2:1 are zinc chromates of definite X-ray structure; the other compositions are merely mixtures of these.

props.name: Zn-rich compositions are effective methanol-synthesis catalysts
props.note: stated as a premise; no synthesis test is reported in this paper
props.statement: As methanol-synthesis catalysts, compositions richer in zinc than chromium are effective, so mainly these were measured by X-ray.

props.name: (A) and (B) are 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O
props.statement: The crystal structures of (A) and (B) were not determined, but taken with the thermal results they are estimated to correspond to the compositions 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O.

props.name: change A is the endothermic desorption of absorbed water
props.statement: Change A (at Zn:Cr 1.5:1) is considered an endothermic change from desorption of water, since hygroscopicity increases as chromium increases beyond 1.5:1.

props.name: the unidentified lines are those of the intermediate oxide Cr2O5
props.statement: The lines seen at 355 and 450 °C are thought to be interference lines of the intermediate oxide Cr2O5, but this has not been confirmed.

props.note: lines belonging to neither CrO3 nor Cr2O3; footnote ※2 suggests an intermediate oxide Cr2O5, not confirmed
